n: In this final group of psalms of David, psalms of praise and wisdom ({{Psalm 138:1-139:24|Psalms 138–139}}, {{Psalm 145:1-21|145}}) form a frame around five psalms of lament ({{Psalm 140:1-144:15|Psalms 140–144}}).

- The psalmist urgently prays for rescue. He does not have incense or an evening offering ({{Exodus 29:38-39|Exodus 29:38–39}}), but his prayers and devotion represent those elements (see {{Isaiah 1:13|Isaiah 1:13}}; {{Revelation 5:8|Revelation 5:8}}). 

- *uplifted hands*: This is a posture of prayer ({{Psalm 28:2|Psalms 28:2}}; {{Psalm 88:9|88:9}}; {{Psalm 143:6|143:6}}; {{Exodus 9:29|Exodus 9:29}}; {{1 Timothy 2:8|1 Timothy 2:8}}).
The psalmist prays for rescue and for wisdom. He also looks ahead to the end of evil. The idea that people receive what they deserve ({{Psalm 141:10|Psalm 141:10}}) holds the psalm together.

- Wisdom sometimes requires protection from oneself. People might say or think things that lead to a harmful path ({{Proverbs 13:3|Proverbs 13:3}}; {{Proverbs 21:23|21:23}}). 

- Wisdom accepts correction from godly people (see {{Proverbs 3:11|Proverbs 3:11}}; {{Proverbs 9:8|9:8}}; {{Proverbs 15:31|15:31}}; {{Proverbs 19:25|19:25}}).
Although overwhelmed by his persecutors ({{Psalm 142:6|Psalm 142:6}}), the psalmist seeks wisdom from the Lord.
*when he was in the cave*: Compare {{Psalm 57:1|Psalm 57:1}}.
He feels trapped and stressed, similar to being in prison (see {{Psalm 107:10|Psalm 107:10}}).

The psalmist feels deep despair (see {{Psalm 77:3|Psalm 77:3}}), and the Lord helps him in his distress. The psalmist trusts in the Lord's wisdom (see {{Psalm 139:1-24|Psalm 139}}) but mourns being trapped by evil people ({{Psalm 5:9-10|5:9–10}}; {{Psalm 140:5|140:5}}; {{Psalm 141:9|141:9}}; {{Psalm 142:3|142:3}}).
Even when alone, the psalmist trusts the Lord, who is his life (see {{Psalm 9:9|Psalms 9:9}}; {{Psalm 16:5|16:5}}; {{Psalm 27:13|27:13}}).
Though overwhelmed by loneliness and trouble, the psalmist focuses on the Lord’s goodness and protection. He knows that the Lord alone is his Redeemer, so he offers his praise.
The psalmist faces severe persecution, so he cries to the Lord, and the Lord will rescue him.
The psalmist prays for God’s love and mercy.

In this lament, the psalmist feels overwhelmed by constant trouble from his enemies, so he turns to the Lord’s love, righteousness, and faithfulness. He remembers what God has done in the past and longs for God to renew his love. He opens himself to God’s wisdom because he knows that God’s instruction leads to life.
Everyone has sinned and is guilty before God ({{Romans 3:20-24|Romans 3:20–24}}).
*My spirit grows faint within me*: The psalmist admits his desperation as his life seems to slip away under cruel and powerful enemies.
Remembering God’s acts from the past reassures the psalmist of God’s faithfulness ({{Psalm 42:4|Psalms 42:4}}; {{Psalm 63:6|63:6}}; {{Psalm 77:3|77:3}}, {{Psalm 77:6|6}}; {{Psalm 119:55|119:55}}).
The psalmist’s thirst is a deep longing for God’s redemption (see {{Psalm 42:1-2|Psalm 42:1–2}}).

The psalmist experiences depression. He describes himself as close to death from sorrow ({{Psalm 31:10|Psalms 31:10}}; {{Psalm 119:87|119:87}}). He feels worn out ({{Psalm 39:10|Psalms 39:10}}; {{Psalm 71:9|71:9}}; {{Psalm 119:81|119:81}}). He is weak from longing ({{Psalm 84:2|Psalm 84:2}}). He feels overwhelmed by the burdens of life ({{Psalm 90:7|Psalm 90:7}}, {{Psalm 90:9|9}}).
The psalmist asks the Lord to renew his love.

- The psalmist prays for wisdom (see {{Psalm 5:8|Psalms 5:8}}; {{Psalm 25:4-6|25:4–6}}; {{Psalm 138:1-8|138}}; {{Psalm 143:10|143:10}}). 

- *Your good Spirit*: The Spirit brings God's goodness (see {{Psalm 23:6|Psalm 23:6}}).
*revive*: Here, it means to bring someone out of despair and restore them to life ({{Psalm 80:19|Psalms 80:19}}; {{Psalm 85:6|85:6}}; {{Psalm 138:7|138:7}}).
The psalm ends with a prayer for God to show that the psalmist is in the right and to restore his life.
*my Rock … my steadfast love … my deliverer … my shield*: The psalmist’s descriptive names for the Lord reveal his deep love for him.

This lament begins with an exclamation of love for the Lord. The community then reflects on the temporary nature of life ({{Psalm 144:3-4|Psalm 144:3–4}}). The psalmist asks for God's help and anticipates victory ({{Psalm 144:5-11|Psalm 144:5–11}}). 

A new song ({{Psalm 144:9-10|Psalm 144:9–10}}) and a prayer for rescue ({{Psalm 144:11|144:11}}) introduce the theme of the Lord’s blessings through his care and protection ({{Psalm 144:12-15|Psalm 144:12–15}}).

*what is man*: The same question in {{Psalm 8:4-6|Psalm 8:4–6}} leads to the answer that humans are only mortal (they do not live forever), yet God gives them honor and responsibility to rule. 

The psalmist focuses on how brief and fragile human life is. He describes it as temporary and passing quickly (see {{Psalm 90:3|Psalms 90:3}}, {{Psalm 90:7-10|7–10}}; {{Psalm 102:11|102:11}}; {{Psalm 109:23|109:23}}; {{Psalm 146:4|146:4}}).
The psalmist asks God to act against his enemies (compare {{Psalm 18:7-19|Psalm 18:7–19}}).
The psalmist compares sons and daughters to plants and pillars, which are images of strength and beauty.

This prayer for the Lord’s blessing brings the laments of {{Psalm 140:1-144:15|Psalms 140–144}}to a close. It describes God’s provision (care for needs) and protection (keeping people safe; see {{Psalm 127:1-5|Psalm 127}}), not only for the psalmist but also for his children and for all who follow God.
*no going into captivity, and no cry of lament*: These images show peace and safety.
The psalmist praises God, the Great King who reigns over all other rulers (see {{Psalm 47:2|Psalm 47:2}}).

This psalm of praise is the last in this collection of the psalms of David ({{Psalm 138:1-145:21|Psalms 138–145}}). Praise continues in the last five psalms ({{Psalm 146:1-150:6|Psalms 146–150}}). 

This psalm celebrates the Lord as the King of all ({{Psalm 145:1-3|Psalm 145:1–3}}, {{Psalm 145:10-13|10–13}}). God's actions show his royal qualities ({{Psalm 145:4-7|Psalm 145:4–7}}). He cares for all creatures ({{Psalm 145:14-17|Psalm 145:14–17}}) and for those who fear him ({{Psalm 145:18-20|145:18–20}}).

This litany (a repeated form of praise, often with the same line said again and again) celebrates God’s character and his mighty deeds. Each generation will continue to tell others about God’s power ({{Psalm 22:30|Psalm 22:30}}).
God consistently demonstrates his character toward all his creation (see {{Psalm 136:25|Psalm 136:25}}).
These verses form a description of the Lord’s kingdom.
The Lord cares for his creatures.

The Lord cares for those who love him and fear him. God-fearers love the Lord and find refuge in him ({{Psalm 5:11|Psalm 5:11}}). They seek him as their only true Savior ({{Psalm 40:16|Psalms 40:16}}; {{Psalm 70:4|70:4}}). They will experience a good future ({{Psalm 69:36|Psalm 69:36}}) and enjoy the peace that God gives ({{Psalm 119:165|119:165}}).

The call to praise ({{Psalm 146:1-2|Psalm 146:1–2}}) leads to a warning against foolishness and false confidence ({{Psalm 146:3-4|146:3–4}}). The psalm ends with a blessing for everyone who places their hope in the Lord ({{Psalm 146:5-7|Psalm 146:5–7}}).

The book of Psalms ends with five poems of praise. These psalms praise God for being the King who rules for ever over everything and everyone. They praise him for being the Maker of everything that exists. They praise him for taking care of every part of creation.

This includes caring for the stars, the weather, the land, plants and animals. It includes making sure that justice is done for needy people. God takes care of outsiders, prisoners, widows and children whose parents have died. He takes care of those who are blind, hungry, helpless or treated badly. He cares deeply for each human being.

Every single creature and thing made by God is able to praise him. Psalm 149 and Psalm 150 talk about ways that human beings praise God. They praise him with their hands. This means that they obey God’s commands. God uses them to bring judgement against those who refuse to respect and obey him.

Humans also praise God with their mouths. This means that their words bring honour and glory to God. They sing songs of praise about God’s work in their lives. These songs were called new songs. They were new because they were based on receiving God’s mercy in new ways. Singing, dancing and playing instruments are some ways that humans praise God. These are ways to show their joy. God’s people can be full of joy because God delights in them and blesses them.
The Psalter ends with five hallelujah psalms, so named because each begins and ends with *Praise the LORD!* (Hebrew *haleluyah*).
Repeating the Lord’s name (shown as LORD in the Berean Standard Bible) four times emphasizes that he alone heals, lifts burdens, loves, and protects.
This verse is a call to worship.
The psalmist calls for the Lord to be praised for restoring and blessing Zion, caring for the poor, displaying his power over nature, and revealing himself to his people.
The psalmist remembers how the Lord restored Jerusalem and brought back his people who had suffered in exile.

- The Lord created the heavens. 

- *He determines the number of the stars*: God's people can feel secure knowing the Lord cares for every detail of his creation. He knows all that belongs to him.
God delivers justice to both the poor and the wicked ({{Psalm 55:22|Psalms 55:22}}; {{Psalm 140:12|140:12}}; {{Psalm 145:14|145:14}}; {{Psalm 146:7|146:7}}).
Human achievements do not impress God, who commands nature. Instead, he finds joy in those who fear him.
God has complete authority and power over the weather ({{Psalm 77:17-18|Psalms 77:17–18}}; {{Psalm 78:26|78:26}}; {{Psalm 104:4|104:4}}; {{Psalm 148:5-6|148:5–6}}).

*the legs of a man*: Any physical or mental strength comes from the Lord, like the strength of a horse. These gifts are reasons to praise the Lord, not to boast ({{Jeremiah 9:23-24|Jeremiah 9:23–24}}).

- *the bars of your gates*: These represent protection from enemies. 

- God blesses his people by giving them safety, prosperity, peace, and the things they need (see {{Psalm 133:3|Psalm 133:3}}).
Simply by speaking his command, the Lord can change the season from harsh winter to refreshing spring (see {{Psalm 147:8|Psalms 147:8}}; {{Psalm 148:5-6|148:5–6}}).
*word … statutes … judgments*: The Lord gave powerful words to Israel so that they might obey him ({{Psalm 105:45|Psalm 105:45}}).

When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the crowds welcomed him like a king and shouted blessings, including a phrase from this verse ({{Matthew 21:9|Matthew 21:9}}; {{Mark 11:10|Mark 11:10}}; {{Luke 19:38|Luke 19:38}}).
This psalm calls for the whole created order to praise the Lord because he has honored his faithful people.
The created order is stable because of the Lord's word (see {{Psalm 33:9|Psalm 33:9}}).

In the ancient Near East, people believed that different gods controlled different parts of nature. But the Lord rules over all of nature. Every part of creation serves him and brings him praise by obeying him ({{Psalm 77:17-18|Psalms 77:17–18}}; {{Psalm 104:4|104:4}}; {{Psalm 135:7|135:7}}; {{Psalm 147:8|147:8}}, {{Psalm 147:15-18|15–18}}; {{Numbers 11:31|Numbers 11:31}}).
The psalmist calls all humans to offer praise to God, regardless of status, age, or gender.

- Praise of the Lord by all people is right because he is glorious and has blessed his people (see {{Psalm 147:13|Psalm 147:13}}; {{Isaiah 46:13|Isaiah 46:13}}; {{Ephesians 3:10|Ephesians 3:10}}). 

- *His saint* are God's trusting and devoted servants ({{Psalm 86:2|Psalm 86:2}}).

This psalm of praise celebrates the Lord's victory. God is the Maker of Israel ({{Psalm 149:1-2|Psalm 149:1–2}}) and the victorious King who shares his glory with his faithful followers ({{Psalm 149:3-9|149:3–9}}).

God’s people, whom the world ignores and looks down on, will be shown to be right ({{Matthew 19:30|Matthew 19:30}}). The humble will overcome those who oppress and persecute them (see {{Isaiah 61:3|Isaiah 61:3}}).
*vengeance*: The Lord is the one who brings justice against wrongdoing (see {{Psalm 2:3|Psalms 2:3}}; {{Psalm 94:1|94:1}}; {{Psalm 102:20|102:20}}; {{Psalm 142:7|142:7}}; {{Psalm 146:7|146:7}}).
The phrase *mighty heavens* refers to {{Genesis 1:1-31|Genesis 1}} and God's amazing work in filling the emptiness.
Everything that breathes is commanded to praise the Lord as he deserves. The whole Psalter describes the greatness of the Lord, so this psalm is a fitting conclusion.

- The psalmist calls all people to praise God with instruments and dancing.

- *flutes*: These are wind instruments (instruments you blow into to make sound). The Bible does not mention them as part of formal temple worship. This suggests they were used more in everyday life or celebrations, rather than in official worship at the temple.

- *clashing cymbals*: Temple musicians clapped two bronze bowls together to make a loud sound as part of the music.
*praise the LORD!*: This refrain is a fitting conclusion to the entire book of Psalms.
